sources.news_title: Trump fans Canada spat by renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump is moving to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, escalating his clash with Canada after trade negotiations between the two nations collapsed.
Trump on Thursday signed a directive changing the name of the lake and said the move would take place “effective immediately.” The president previewed the move in a social media post earlier this week. The order signed by Trump said the Interior Department had 30 days to change the name in federal databases and materials.
“Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade,” Trump told reporters when asked what message he was sending to the U.S.’s northern neighbor. “They want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that anymore.”

sources.news_title: Trump renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ amid growing tensions with Canada
sources.text:
Trump renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ amid growing tensions with Canada
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said on Thursday he was renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” amid growing tensions between Canada and the United States.
He signed an executive order directing the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the US geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow his preferred naming convention, however.
Trump has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the US announced it was imposing 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down.
Trump has been needling America’s northern neighbor since he returned to the White House last year, suggesting the ally with whom the US once had warm relations should instead be absorbed as the 51st state.
Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read “Lake America.”
On the other side of the president was another map with the words, “MAKING THE GREAT LAKES EVEN GREATER.”
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” he wrote.
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston dismissed Trump’s move in a social media post, writing: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
The lake is one of multiple Great Lakes that the US and Canada share borders along. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat whose state shares a border on the lake, wrote on X in response to the White House’s announcement that, “New York won’t be calling it that.”
There is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water and Trump has wide latitude over how the US government recognizes geographic places and landmarks.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has traded insults with Trump, this week brushed aside the prospect of Trump changing the lake’s name as “a lot of rhetoric.”
The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Trump said that while his action was not meant to send any particular geopolitical message, “Canada’s been ripping us off for a long time” on trade and military issues.
“They wanted to be treated like a state and they’re not a state,” the president said. “We just can’t do that anymore.”
“We love the people of Canada,” Trump added. “I don’t think their representatives do, an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference.”
The move is reminiscent of his move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”

Lake Ontario's Name To Remain "Now And Always": Canada's Carney Slams Trump
PM Carney challenges Trump’s order to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
sources.text: U.S. President Donald Trump has signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s executive order, reaffirming that no matter what the U.S. calls it, Canadians will know it as “Lake Ontario – then, now and always.” The news comes after a public spat between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, as the U.S. imposed tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian goods and Trump threatened 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian autos. The federal government has since responded with dollar-for-dollar tariffs that will come into effect after Labour Day. Key details: Here’s everything that happened on Aug. 27, 2026: Trump says Lake renaming is ‘effective immediately’ U.S. President Donald Trump has signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” Trump made the announcement in the Oval Office Thursday afternoon. Trump said the move was “official, effective immediately” and that his administration has “filed all the necessary papers, documents” and “notified all of the various people that we have to notify.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘Lake Ontario – then, now and always’: PM Carney Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s executive order on Thursday, reaffirming that no matter what the U.S. calls it, Canadians will know it as “Lake Ontario – then, now and always.” “The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney posted on social media on Thursday afternoon. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he continued. Carney highlighted that the United States is changing “their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments and their hydronyms,” but that “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Can Trump rename Lake Ontario? CTV News’ chief political correspondent Vassy Kapelos answered the question on a lot of Canadians’ minds: Can Trump change the name of Lake Ontario? “The short answer is yes and no,” Kapelos explained Thursday after Trump’s announcement. “He can do what he wants as far as what the United States is able to, or wants to, or decides to call any body of water or any landmark,” she said. “But he cannot dictate what Canadians call that body of water, or maybe more importantly … what the international community or other countries call it.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist How did Lake Ontario get its name? The name is older than Canada itself. Historians believe Lake Ontario’s name has Iroquoian roots meaning “beautiful lake” or “sparkling water,” according to the Canadian Encyclopedia. Europeans began calling the lake “Ontario” in 1641, the encyclopedia entry says, and by 1656 the name was appearing on maps. The province of Ontario is named after the lake. The Canadian Press Read the full story here U.S. Board of Geographic Names ordered to rename lake U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued an official order to the U.S. Board of Geographic Names to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” Burgum shared the order in a social media post on Thursday with the caption “Make the Great Lakes Great Again!” “The area formally known as Lake Ontario has long been an integral asset to America, as a critical artery for America’s early trade and commerce, and as a vital economic resource for America,” the order said. “President Trump has directed the change in the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, and the BGN must immediately take steps to accomplish the President’s instructions,” the document read. “This order is effective immediately.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Trump claims ‘Lake America’ name change official Trump posted a letter on Truth Social which declared that Lake Ontario is now “Lake America.” “As of 4:30 pm today the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) has officially designated the former Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America in all official USGS electronic documents,” a letter from USGS director Ned Mamula read, which Trump posted on Truth Social. The letter added that printed documents will reflect the change in “the next several days.” Trump also posted a map with “Lake America” in large bold red letters highlighting Lake Ontario. ‘Not his best work’: Kinew on Trump Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew responded to Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, telling reporters the move is not the U.S. president’s “best work.” “You know when a rock band is really over the hill, and you see them in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago?” he said. “I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now.” Kinew said Trump “thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie,” when he renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” in January 2025, and “he’s trying (to) bring back that and he’s trying to play the hits for his base.” “But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work,” he added. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Ontario’s Ford weighs in on Trump order Ontario Premier Doug Ford weighed in on Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, echoing what Carney and other Canadian politicians have said. “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” Ford wrote in a post on social media. Earlier this week, during an appearance on Bloomberg TV, Ford said it was up to Trump if he wanted to change it, but Canadians will “always going to call it Lake Ontario.” Bryann Aguilar, CP24.com journalist ‘Sad and pathetic’: U.S. officials condemn Trump Several U.S. politicians are criticizing Trump’s proposed renaming of Lake Ontario, calling it “pathetic” and a “distraction” from failed trade talks. Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an Independent who regularly votes with Democrats, called out Trump for cutting health care, child care, housing, education and nutrition assistance in a social media post criticizing the “Lake America” order. Former U.S. secretary of state Hillary Clinton, who ran against Trump as the Democratic presidential candidate in 2016, chimed in on Thursday’s executive order, posting to social media that “It’s Lake Ontario.” New York’s Chuck Schumer, the U.S. Senate minority leader, called the order “sad and pathetic” on social media. “Voters will respond accordingly in November,” he warned. Joe Van Wonderen, CTVNews.ca journalist Read the full story here ‘They feel entitled’ Trump says about Canada When asked by reporters why he’s so focused on America’s ally, Trump said “they haven’t treated us well.” “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people. They charge our farmers 400 per cent tariffs,” Trump responded. “People oftentimes, they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with… and I said that’s easy: Canada. They are the worst, and they feel entitled, and just we can’t have that.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Trump: Canada ‘ripping us off for a long time’ When asked what message Trump is attempting to send to Canada with the renaming, the president reiterated that Canada has been “ripping us off for a long time on trade.” “Very sadly, even the military. You know, we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything. They don’t pay us to defend Canada, but we defend Canada, and they understand that,” he told reporters. Trump brought up 11 brand new icebreakers as an example of his grievances. “They’d like to use the icebreakers. They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘Do I care about how the Québécois speak?’ Lutnick says U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick claims the U.S. did not raise issues with the French language or the Québécois in trade negotiation talks with Canada last week. “If you think I ever said the words ‘French,’ do I care about how the Quebecois speak?” he said to reporters in Washington on Thursday. “I mean, what could matter less to America? We don’t care. So, the fact is, we never brought those words up.” Lutnick claims the detail was “manufactured” by Prime Minister Mark Carney to end negotiations with the U.S. “There’s the sovereignty party trying to run, and they’re in the lead in Quebec, and so this was Mark manufacturing something that would try to keep them from winning.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘The math was sensational’: Lutnick “We’re just being used by them,” Lutnick told reporters about Canada’s decision to end trade talks. “That’s why it ended. It didn’t happen for math. The math was sensational,” he said. “It was a great deal that we shook hands on.” Lutnick also claimed that concerns about medium- to heavy-duty trucks were strategically held by Canada until the last moment in trade negotiations. Despite meeting with LeBlanc 10 times and speaking to Carney twice, “the words ‘medium’ and ‘heavy-duty trucks’ were raised in these trade negotiations at Friday at 4:00,” he added. “These were things they put in in order to make it end,” he said. “It was nonsense.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Canada replacing seafood counter-tariffs with other items The federal government is replacing its counter-tariffs on seafood with 50 per cent levies on a series of other American goods, according to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s office. “This decision was made in the interest of strengthening Canada’s sectors and our tariff response — and to better match the American tariffs dollar for dollar, rate for rate,” Champagne’s press secretary John Fragos wrote in a statement to CTV News, adding the federal government has been consulting with stakeholders and provinces when it comes to counter-tariff options. Fragos also tells CTV News that the decision to remove seafood from Canada’s list of counter-tariffs was made in part to avoid giving the appearance of escalation by Canada in the face of a simmering trade conflict with the United States, as the U.S. does not tariff Canadian seafood imports. Newly added to Canada’s list of counter-tariffs include: Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer and Stephanie Ha, CTV News Ottawa National Bureau manager Read the full story here Trump ‘hell-bent’ on ending Canada-U.S. friendship: Reid According to CTV News political commentator Scott Reid, Trump’s executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America shows how unserious he is. “People make jokes about it, I’ve made jokes about it, but it isn’t really funny,” Reid, who once served as director of communications for former prime minister Paul Martin, told CTV News Channel on Thursday. “He’s treating it like it’s a clown show,” he added. The last time Trump attempted to rename an international body of water, changing the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America,” it was largely ignored by domestic and international media. “I guess this is what makes Donald Trump feel good about being Donald Trump, but all that signals to serious people on either side of the border, is that the president isn’t serious,” Reid said.He added that it shows the U.S. president doesn’t take his job, people’s income, or trade seriously. “Donald Trump is hell-bent on making sure Canada is not a friend and does not become a friend again anytime soon. That appears to be his mission,” Reid said. Joe Van Wonderen, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘We are still going to call it Lake Ontario’: Brampton mayor Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown told CNN on Thursday afternoon that Trump’s efforts to rename Lake Ontario are a “bit preposterous” and are mostly being laughed off in Canada. “We are still going to call it Lake Ontario, I think many of you will still call it Lake Ontario. The only person who is going to have trouble with what to call it is your president,” Brown said. “Just like if our prime minister wanted to rename the Mississippi (River) you might get a bit of a chuckle out of it. It is having the same reaction in Canada.” Brown is the latest in a line of Ontario politicians to appear on CNN and other U.S. television networks in recent days to make a direct appeal to Americans. The Brampton mayor said the trade war is “not something Canada has sought” and that it has “bewildered” most Canadians. “The only people sipping champagne right now are our competitors from Asia and the EU who look at this chaos in North America as an opportunity to increase market share,” he said. Chris Fox, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist ‘Just doesn’t seem very serious’: political analyst A U.S. political analyst told CTV News Channel on Thursday that Americans found the proposed renaming of Lake Ontario confusing and laughable. “It’s a mixture of laughter and of raised eyebrows, wondering when the other shoe is going to drop,” said Jeffrey Bloodworth, a political analyst at Gannon University. “Its one thing to rename a lake, and people kind of laugh,” he said, adding “normal regular people” are wondering “what the heck is going on, because this just doesn’t seem very serious.” Bloodworth highlighted that although the move may appear “comical,” hundreds of billions of dollars of commerce flow through the border. If Trump continues to upset the trading relationship, it could have damaging effects on people’s livelihoods, he said. “Most people expect this is kind of political theatre that will be retracted,” he said. Joe Van Wonderen, CTVNews.ca journalist Quebec manufacturer blames tariffs for closure As Canada’s forestry industry comes under attack from the trade war with the United States, a Quebec paperboard manufacturer says it is closing — putting more than 400 people out of work. The RYAM industrial complex in Temiscaming, Que., will close in September, officials announced Thursday. The company said business has become unsustainable with 50 per cent tariffs targeting the Canadian forest industry. Temiscaming Mayor Alain Gauthier said the tariffs are a “nuclear bomb” for sectors that rely on U.S. markets. “It’s an economic war,” he said. “We plan for every option. We’re not naïve. For the short-term, we need a bridge to get across that river.” Eric Taschner, CTVNewsNorthernOntario.ca journalist Read the full story here Tariff confusion impacting B.C. business A B.C. outdoor living company says confusion over tariffs has some American customers thinking twice about hitting the “buy” button, even though its products remain exempt from the taxes. About 82 per cent of GOODLAND’s business comes from the United States and most transactions are done online. Craig Pearce of the Vancouver-based company told CTV News that when customers see “Proudly Canadian” on the website, they often assume they’ll have to pay a steep tariff, when they don’t. “I think there’s a trickle-down effect, right? It’s just the confusion, uncertainty,” said Pearce. He admitted the constantly changing tariff lists makes it difficult to know what could be affected next. St. John Alexander, CTV News Vancouver journalist Read the full story here ‘Shop Canadian’ app sees surge in use A “Shop Canadian” app created by two Edmontonians is seeing an uptick in traffic, with the creators crediting the sudden patriotism directly to Canada’s relationship with the U.S. The app, launched in January 2025 by William Boytinck and Matthew Suddaby, is a 10,000-company database that allows consumers to scan most barcodes while shopping to see whether a product is locally or nationally made. Each trade announcement leads to a slight bump in traffic on the app, Boytinck said. The U.S.-Canada trade war has contributed to one of the app’s most “noticeable” bumps yet, with 30,000 requests for product information since last week. “I think it’s just from people who want to support local businesses and do their parts,” Boytinck added. Hannah Kavanagh, CTVNewsEdmonton.ca digital journalist Read the full story here Chapman’s vows no price increase Canadian ice cream manufacturer Chapman’s has promised to not increase prices for almost two years amid the ongoing trade war with the U.S. In a social media post Wednesday, Chapman’s vowed to keep prices as they are until March 2028. “We will continue to support our employees with a living wage and provide our customers with the best product for the best price, using only 100% Canadian dairy,” the ice cream maker said. Chapman’s called Trump’s tariffs “unjustified” and said it stands with the Canadian government and all provinces. The company said it’s also on track to convert 70 per cent of its American ingredients by mid-2027. Chapman’s ended the post with a strong call for Canadians to “buy” and “support” Canadian. Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist Toronto mayor reinforces ‘buy local’ initiative Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow is reminding residents to support local businesses and buy Canadian as the ongoing trade war threatens to drive up costs for everyday Canadians. Speaking at a news conference, Chow warned that families could feel the impact at the grocery store, saying “the prices could go up again” as tariffs continue to affect trade between Canada and the U.S. “This is how we Canadians respond to this senseless trade war,” Chow said, calling on residents to “stand up for each other” by buying and investing locally. Chow also highlighted the city’s efforts to support local companies through its EDGE Incentive Program, which provides property tax relief to eligible businesses that expand and create jobs. In a news release, the city says National Dry Beverages, the first company approved under the program, is investing $18.1 million to add about 62,000 square feet of industrial space to its Arrow Road facility. The expansion is expected to create 20 full-time jobs and increase the company’s permanent workforce by nearly 40 per cent. Since launching in January 2025, Chow says the EDGE program has approved eight projects representing about $220 million in construction investment, 583 projected new jobs and 725 retained jobs. Chow said the city is also using its purchasing power to support Canadian companies, with 98 per cent of its spending last year already going to Canadian businesses. “Trump’s trade war is just bad business,” she added. Jermaine Wilson, CP24.com and CTVNews.ca journalist Trump renames Lake Ontario in video A video posted to U.S. President Donald Trump’s Instagram page shows him crossing out a map of Lake Ontario and renaming it “Lake America.” The video shared Wednesday night shows Trump sitting in the Oval Office with a map of the lake. “We’re going to make a little change,” he says in the video. “We’re going to call it something different than Lake Ontario. We’re going to call it Lake America.” “All it takes is a good pen and some intelligence,” the president added. With a black pen, Trump is seen crossing out the name and writing a new one. “Lake Ontario, that’s gone,” he says, looking at the camera. “So, now we have a lake and now we have a gulf, because we have the Gulf of America and now we have Lake America.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist He’s kidding about renaming Lake Ontario, right Trump’s latest attempt to claim U.S. sovereignty over Lake Ontario is the latest in a long line of attacks against Canada that will make it harder for political will to galvanize around a trade agreement. You might think his remarks are simply bluster, maybe even a joke, coming from a former reality television star. But in the aftermath of Venezuela, his incremental efforts at overtaking Greenland and his six-month war in Iran, the president is proving his authoritarian bent is very much serious — and it’s playing out in very stark terms throughout the latest negotiations with Canada. Eric Ham, CTV News political analyst in Washington No tariffs on U.S. seafood, fish: Finance Canada Canada will no longer tariff U.S. fish and seafood products. Finance Canada released a statement on X late Wednesday saying it made the change to protect against “broader economic harms” and after the federal government received feedback from Canadian industries. The statement added that it is making some adjustments to the list of counter-tariffs. It did not say what the other changes are. The Canadian Press U.S. drops Canadian culture from talks Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says the United States will not target promotion of the French language or Canadian culture in ongoing actions around trade. “Canada welcomes that the U.S. is now withdrawing its positions on discoverability and labelling and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future U.S. trade actions,” LeBlanc said in a social media post. “We look forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty.” LeBlanc’s statement came in response to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s comments to CBC News on Wednesday, in which he said discoverability of French content was discussed during trade talks, but not as a deal-breaker. Earlier on Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump called the idea of him interfering with Canadians speaking French a “stupid thing,” in a post on social media. Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘Venezuela of the north’ In a CNN interview earlier today, Canada’s former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland said Trump’s latest salvos aimed at Canada are about “dominance,” and “trying to turn Canada from a partner and an ally into a vassal. It’s trying to turn Canada into the Venezuela of the north.” She said Canada won’t give up its sovereignty. “We want to be America’s friend. We want to be your ally. But we’re not going to be your servant,” said Freeland. The Trump administration tried getting through the back door what they couldn’t get through the front door. CUSMA, which was negotiated by Trump in his first term, made it difficult for the White House to fully enact an ‘economic warfare’ framework that would bring Canada into subjectivity. Therefore, the president sought to force an agreement on Ottawa that would see the Great White North give up its independence and sovereignty. Trump will eventually cave, but that doesn’t mean an improved trade agreement is forthcoming. Both nations will likely remain at status quo as Washington once again exhibits it can’t be trusted. This will make the second war this White House has lost. First, the war in Iran, and now a stunning and ill-advised trade war with its biggest trading partner and one of its oldest allies. Eric Ham, CTV News political analyst in Washington Trump trade war with Canada costing him in Michigan In the state of Michigan, 40 per cent or roughly US$70 billion in goods are imported annually from Canada. The Great White North is Michigan’s largest trading partner. Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed stated on the campaign trail after talks broke down: “You gotta be an asshole to pick a trade war with Canada.” The state has been Ground Zero for President Trump’s continued attacks on Canada. Now, however, voters appear willing to elevate El-Sayed over his Republican challenger as the Michigan economy looks to come to a grinding halt as the trade war between the U.S. and Canada heats up. Eric Ham, CTV News political analyst in Washington Americans push to get back to table We’re continuing to see key sectors call for both sides to come back to the negotiating table. Already the powerful U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the U.S. Business Council have implored talks to continue. At a more local level, in the state of Maine, a jurisdiction that could shape the balance of power in Washington, the Maine Lobsters Association is also pushing for talks between Washington and Ottawa to continue. Republican U.S. Senator Susan Collins is locked in a heated battle for re-election and the trade war has placed Canada at the top of the ballot for voters in that state. Eric Ham, CTV News political analyst in Washington No renegotiations in short term: adviser A Canada-U.S. relations adviser says she doesn’t think trade negotiations will resume any time soon. “I don’t have much hope,” Lisa Raitt, former deputy leader for the Conservative party, told CTV Your Morning on Thursday. There would need to be an “external factor” that would prompt both sides to return to the table, Raitt added. For example, trade negotiations halted last October despite being close to a deal and only resumed this July. Although negotiations halted again last week, the relationship between both parties was “professional,” Raitt said she was told. She said she doesn’t know if there are ongoing conversations between Canada and the U.S. on a deal. “For the moment, we are seeing a war of words in the media, which is unfortunate.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘Havoc’ for private investment: economist An economist says uncertainty from the trade war is causing “havoc” for private investment into Canada. “Not on the consumer product side,” Pedro Antunes, chief economist of Signal 49 Research, answered when asked if Canada is currently attractive to investors. Canada’s manufacturing sector was appealing due to its access to the U.S., he told CTV Your Morning on Thursday. “That’s a different story.” Antunes said Canada may see better outcomes with resource investment.“A lot of our resources now (come) from a secure place,” he said. He added that it may be “advantageous” to lean on Canada’s critical minerals to attract investors. Canada needs to show “success” on getting major projects rolling and approved quickly, Antunes said. “That will be attractive to investors again for all of the reasons ... safe place, lots of resources, a stable government.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Previous days’ updates follow: Saskatchewan’s Moe announces 50% tariff on U.S. liquor Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says his government will be imposing a 50 per cent reciprocal tax on alcohol from the United States. Moe said the trade measures will be implemented Sept. 8. “Given the increased tariffs that the United States of America has put on Canadian and Saskatchewan goods, given the counter tariffs that are in place, we need to protect ourselves,” Moe said. The premier says the province is not considering pulling U.S. booze from shelves, noting his government is adamant on leaving the choice up to consumers. “That is a very core value for this government to allow Saskatchewan people to make their own choice,” Moe said. David Prisciak, CTVNewsRegina.ca digital journalist Read the full story here Smith urges de-escalation of trade war Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. signals a need to accelerate timelines on major national projects and business relief. On Wednesday, Smith doubled down on her aversion to oil and gas export tariffs to retaliate against recently imposed U.S. tariffs, which she called “tragic, unjustified, and wholly unnecessary.” Tariffs are expected to affect about $1.5 billion of Alberta exports to the south. Oil and gas and beef cattle — Alberta’s biggest industries — are so far unaffected. “Rather than making threats and promises we know we cannot keep, Canada should focus on what we can control and do,” Smith said. Hannah Kavanagh, CTVNewsEdmonton.ca digital journalist Read the full story here Smith puts political interests ahead of Canada: Mulcair Smith is putting her political interests ahead of a united Canadian response to the trade war with the United States, says CTV News political commentator Tom Mulcair. “She’s trying to mollycoddle the extremists around her, in her home province, and it’s really not coming out very well,” he said in an interview with CTV News Channel Wednesday. Mulcair also dismissed Smith’s explanation that her opposition to Ottawa’s approach is driven by concerns over Ontario’s reliance on U.S. oil and natural gas. “Come on. sources.news_title: Lake Ontario ‘now and always,’ Carney says after Trump ‘Lake America’ order
sources.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said the name of Lake Ontario will remain “now and always” after U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order that he said would have the U.S. refer to the Great Lake as “Lake America,” his latest shot at Canada after trade talks fell apart last week.
Trump, speaking in the Oval Office after signing the order, took the opportunity to once again criticize Canada’s trade policies and leadership but insisted he loves the country and that renaming Lake Ontario was not about sending a message.
“No message,” he told reporters. “As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly. Even the military — you know, we defend Canada for nothing, we don’t get anything.
“They’re not a state, but they want to be treated like they’re a state. And so we just can’t do that anymore,” he added. “We love the people of Canada. I don’t think their representatives do an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change, I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference.”
The U.S. president equated the move to his order for the U.S. to call the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” last year — a move that has not been recognized by the rest of the world. Even U.S.-based Google has opted to put the “Gulf of America” name in parenthesis after the original name in Google Maps.
Carney noted in a statement that the name Lake Ontario is over 400 years old and “comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.'”
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney said on social media.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Experts have told Global News that Canada and the rest of the world are under no obligation to recognize Trump’s new order, noting the name Lake Ontario appeared on maps more than a century before the U.S. declared independence and long before there was a province called Ontario.
“It’s ridiculous on a number of levels,” Daniel Macfarlane, an environmental historian at Western Michigan University and author of The Lives of Lake Ontario, told Global News in an earlier interview.
“Trump really doesn’t even have the capability to actually rename it in a meaningful way without Canadian consent.”
Trump said Tuesday the U.S. was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario as relations with Canada, and particularly Ontario, sour. He later posted a graphic depicting the Great Lake under the proposed “Lake America” name, as well as a TikTok video of himself crossing out Lake Ontario with a Sharpie on a printed-out map and writing “Lake America” overtop.
Get daily National news
The move came after Ontario Premier Doug Ford lashed out at Trump over his new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods and the collapse of trade talks, calling the U.S. president a “loser,” a “bully” and a “dictator.”
“The lake change, ‘Lake of America,’ is something I’ve been thinking about for a long time, actually,” Trump said Thursday. “As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it’s very routinely the ‘Gulf of America.’
“If you think about it, we have a gulf, we have a lake, now all we need is an ocean. So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”
Asked why he was taking such actions against American allies rather than its adversaries, Trump replied: “Well they haven’t treated us very well,” referring to Canadian government officials.
“They’re nasty people,” he said, adding they’re “the worst to deal with on trade” and “feel entitled.”
Canadian officials were quick to slam Trump’s order Thursday.
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them in a casino playing some song from, like, 50 years ago? I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told reporters at an unrelated press conference in Winnipeg.
“He thought he had a real hit, a real ‘golden oldie’ with the Gulf of Mexico, and he’s trying to bring back that. He’s trying to play the hits for his base, but I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston posted on X: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
Trump’s executive order says the U.S. lays claim to most of the “volume” of Lake Ontario and is mostly responsible for its security, economic activity and environmental stewardship.
“The United States has invested nearly $4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade, while Canada has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period,” the document says.
“The Lake will continue to play a pivotal role in shaping America’s future and the global economy. In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America.”
Macfarlane pointed out that the Canadian side of Lake Ontario is actually “far more populated” than the American side in upstate New York, which is “more or less the U.S. backwoods” other than the city of Rochester.
The lake, along with the St. Lawrence River, is “sort of the centre of the original Canada,” he added.
“It’s far more important to Canada than it is to the United States, which on top of the difficulty of how you would even rename it, it just doesn’t really even make logical sense,” Macfarlane said.
“I think it’s just his usual buffoonery tactics.”
The order directs U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to work with the Board on Geographic Names to ensure all U.S. federal government references to Lake Ontario, “including on executive department and agency maps, contracts, and other documents and communications,” reflect Trump’s name change.
“We’re on it, Mr. President!,” Burgum posted on social media, adding he and the U.S. Geological Survey were “PROUD” to implement the order.
“The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States,” he wrote.
As governor of North Dakota, which borders Canada, Burgum often spoke about the “crucial” need to ensure a strong relationship, pointing out that Canada is the state’s largest trading partner “by far.”
Democrats, who are running to take control of Congress in November’s midterm elections, lambasted the move for not addressing Americans’ priorities.
“Donald Trump picked a fight with Canada that is costing you money. Instead of fixing it, he is spending your tax dollars to rename Lake Ontario,” U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries posted on X.
“Republicans don’t give a damn about making your life more affordable.”
U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Trump was putting his own grievances first and “Americans last.”
“Inflation increasing. The Iran war raging on with no end in sight. A trade war with Canada. And what does Trump want? To rename Lake Ontario,” he wrote on social media.

sources.news_title: Mark Carney Gives Trump Reality Check on Lake Ontario Rename
sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed back sharply on Thursday after President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” responding with a pointed reminder of the lake’s deep historical roots.
Within hours of Trump’s order, Carney rejected the change outright, citing the name’s Indigenous origins and more than 400 years of history before insisting Canadians would continue to call it Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney wrote on X.
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.”
The prime minister then appeared to take aim at the sweeping shifts unfolding in the United States under Trump’s leadership.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he wrote.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Carney’s response followed Trump’s Oval Office signing from behind the Resolute Desk, where the president directed the Interior Department to use “Lake America” as the lake’s official name for US federal purposes.
President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney are locked in an increasingly bitter dispute over trade – and now over what to call Lake Ontario
Trump signed an executive order directing the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’
Carney responded by pointing out that the name Lake Ontario has existed for more than 400 years and predates both Canadian Confederation and US independence
The president cannot compel Canada or international organizations to adopt the new name but Trump’s action triggered fury from liberals and delight among MAGA supporters.
Trump put pen to paper in the Oval Office on Thursday, declaring the name change effective immediately as his increasingly bitter trade war with America’s northern neighbor spilled onto the map.
The move instantly became another political flashpoint, with Trump supporters hailing it as masterful trolling while critics branded the president a ‘child,’ a ‘moron’, accusing him of turning the United States into a ‘national embarrassment.’
Trump appeared to relish the controversy as he signed the order.
‘I guess the purpose of this, more than anything else, is we’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately to Lake America,’ he said. ‘That’s going to take place right now as I sign the order.’
The president said he had contemplated the change for a ‘long time’ and suggested he may not be finished tinkering with the map – joking that the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean could eventually find itself in his sights.
‘Actually, as you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico and we changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America,’ Trump said.
‘So, if you think about it, we have a Gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific.’
A map labeling Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ is displayed after Trump signed an executive order in the Oval Office of the White House on Thursday
A poster shows the name change from Lake Ontario to Lake America
Republicans were quick to celebrate the move to rename Lake Ontario
The order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and his department to update the federal Geographic Names Information System to reflect the new US designation.
‘We’re on it, Mr. President!’ Burgum wrote on X. ‘The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States.’
Lake Ontario forms part of the international boundary between New York and the Canadian province of Ontario and has been jointly managed under the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty for more than a century.
Trump nevertheless emphasized the large portion of the lake bordering the United States as he championed his new name.
His supporters quickly embraced the move.
‘THE LAKE AMERICA TROLL JUST BECAME AN EXECUTIVE ORDER,’ conservative commentator Glenn Beck wrote after previously describing the idea as ‘top tier’ trolling.
Trump supporters quickly celebrated the ‘Lake America’ executive order on social media, with conservative commentator Glenn Beck calling the idea ‘top tier’ trolling
But the reaction from Trump’s opponents was blistering.
‘This is why we can’t have nice things,’ Democratic California Rep. Ted Lieu wrote on X.
Senator Bernie Sanders dismissed the rebranding and urged Trump to concentrate instead on issues affecting Americans at home.
‘No, President Trump. The American people don’t want to rename Lake Ontario Lake America,’ Sanders wrote, before calling on the administration to focus on healthcare and other domestic priorities.
Journalist John Harwood was even more scathing, describing those behind the move as ‘Pitiful morons.’
Bulwark editor Sonny Bunch wrote: ‘Anyone who unironically calls Lake Ontario “Lake America” should be ruthlessly mocked. Dumbest sh*t imaginable.’
The announcement comes at a particularly explosive moment in US-Canadian relations.
Trade negotiations between the longtime allies have collapsed, with Trump threatening punishing new tariffs on Canadian goods and Carney promising Canada will retaliate ‘dollar for dollar.’
Trump has said tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel will rise to 50 percent by 2027 as he attempts to force more manufacturing into the United States.
Critics of Trump’s executive order ridiculed the new name online suggesting the president was not focusing on the country’s priorities
And while signing Thursday’s order, the president made clear that his dispute with Ottawa was far bigger than the name of a lake.
‘The whole Canadian thing … has to come to a stop,’ Trump said. ‘We are going to be doing tariffs on their cars that are coming in at a substantial level because we want to make the cars here.
‘They can make their own cars if they want and they can continue to make cars for Canada but we don’t want them to make cars for the United States of America. It’s very simple. Likewise many other products.’
Trump also accused Canada of relying on the United States for military protection without adequately compensating Washington.
‘We defend Canada for nothing, we don’t get anything,’ he said. ‘We love the people of Canada, but their representatives aren’t doing an appropriate job.’
The president has separately branded Canadian officials ‘nasty people’ and described the country as one of America’s most difficult trading partners.
‘People oftentimes they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with on trade, and I said that’s easy, Canada,’ Trump said.
‘They are the worst to trade, and they feel entitled, and just we can’t have that.’
Carney, meanwhile, has been increasingly combative toward Washington as the dispute escalates.

By MICHELLE L. PRICE and WILL WEISSERT, The Associated Press
President Donald Trump said Thursday he is renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States as he escalates his trade war with Canada.
The Republican president signed an executive order directing the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow along, however.
Trump has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down.
Trump has been needling America’s northern neighbor since he returned to the White House last year, suggesting the ally with whom the U.S. once had warm relations should instead be absorbed as the 51st state.
Canada responded to Trump’s import taxes this week by imposing retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.
Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read “Lake America.”
On the other side of the president was another map with the words, “MAKING THE GREAT LAKES EVEN GREATER.”
Trump said as he was signing the order that he’d “notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So, we’ve done everything that you have to do.””And this is official, effective immediately,” he added.
But the executive order Trump signed shows that the changes are supposed to be made within 30 days.
Canadian officials dismissed Trump’s move.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” he wrote.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has traded insults with Trump, said on X: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said, “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
The lake is one of multiple Great Lakes that the U.S. and Canada share borders along. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat whose state shares a border on the lake, wrote on X in response to the White House’s announcement that, “New York won’t be calling it that.”
There is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water and Trump has wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks. Late Thursday, Google maps had not renamed the lake as it did last year after Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico to be renamed the Gulf of America.
The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Trump said that while his action was not meant to send any particular geopolitical message, “Canada’s been ripping us off for a long time” on trade and military issues.
“They wanted to be treated like a state and they’re not a state,” the president said. “We just can’t do that anymore.”
“We love the people of Canada,” Trump added. “I don’t think their representatives do, an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference.”
Trump scribbled his name with a Sharpie pen on the executive order, then held it up for the cameras, offering, “And we filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else.”
He also suggested his push to rename bodies of water may not be finished.
“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump said. “So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them.”— Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto contributed to this report.

sources.text:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney clapped back Thursday against U.S. President Donald Trump’s claim that he is changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” saying Canada won’t bow to that order.
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’,” Carney posted on social media.
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul bluntly dissed Trump’s move on X: “New York won’t be calling it that.”
Premier Doug Ford likewise posted: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
Trump signed an executive order Thursday that he said changed the Great Lake’s name to “Lake America,” making good on a threat after the collapse of trade talks and in retaliation for Canada launching a new round of counter-tariffs against American products.
His move came on a day when Canada walked back its proposed 25 per cent levies on American seafood and fish and swapped in 50 per cent tariffs on some copper and construction materials, even as some analysts said Canada’s plan does not match the impact of the Trump tariffs.
Impactful or not, Canada’s retaliation has infuriated Trump, whose White House posted the name change on social media, prompting a wave of bemused and amused scorn in Canada.
“Lake Ontario is and will always be Lake Ontario, and no executive order will change that,” Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a written statement on X. “It doesn’t belong to President Donald Trump to rename on a whim.”
Poilievre urged Canada to remain focused on the “real trade issues that impact our people. Instead of responding to stunts and distractions, Canadians must stay focused on what we can control: making our economy strong and affordable at home and using our leverage to fight tariffs abroad.”
Trump told reporters at the White House on Thursday that Canada is “the worst to deal with on trade,” and complained about its political leadership.
“Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference. But we can’t let the whole Canadian thing has been going on for decades, and it has to come to a stop,” Trump said as he brandished his executive order renaming Lake Ontario.
“They want to be treated like a state but they’re not a state.”
He went on to rail against Canada for not pulling its weight on defence, for a familiar litany of other trade complaints, and for getting more benefit out of the trading relationship than the U.S. gets. “We just can’t do it anymore,” he said.
Trump reiterated his plan to raise his current 25 per cent tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and automotive parts to 50 per cent as of Jan. 1.
“We’re going to be doing tariffs on their cars that are coming in at a substantial level because we want to make the cars here,” Trump said.
“They can continue to make their cars for Canada, but … we don’t want them to make cars for the United States of America. It’s very simple. Likewise, many other products. So the lake change, the Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time.”
Last year, in one of his first acts in his second term as president, Trump similarly ordered U.S. federal agencies to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.” On Google Maps, that name change is reflected with Gulf of Mexico in brackets.
Two days after laying out Canada’s “targeted, strategic” counterpunch to Trump’s latest 50 per cent tariffs, the Carney government walked back its proposed 25 per cent levies on American seafood and fish late Wednesday night, as some analysts said Canada’s plan does not match the impact of the new U.S. tariffs.
The decision to drop the planned 25 per cent counter-tariff on U.S. fish and seafood largely affects imports from Maine and Alaska, but also protects fish processing plants in Atlantic Canada that package American products like lobster.
Ottawa’s move, which adjusts the overall package announced Tuesday, reflects just how politically sensitive Canada’s decisions are, and how outsized impacts can be on some economic sectors, while raising the question of just how far Canada can go to hit American products without hurting Canadian communities.
After the Finance Department adjusted the list of Canada’s newest counter-tariffs, Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson underscored how hard Atlantic Canadian fishing communities would have been hit.
On Thursday morning, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne defended the move, telling reporters in Toronto that “we made the update because I think that was the right thing to do in the interest of Canada.”
Champagne said the counter-tariff list is intended to “measured” and “targeted.” Asked what message the counter-tariffs send to American trade negotiators, Champagne said it should be no surprise that Canada would respond to the latest U.S. tariffs, but that Ottawa is not seeking to escalate the trade war.
The fish and seafood counter-tariffs were replaced with ones on American construction materials and copper products to retain what the Carney government has called a “dollar-for-dollar” response to a 50 per cent tariff Trump imposed last week on about $27.6 billion worth of Canadian imports to the U.S.
If Trump has his way with Lake Ontario he wouldn’t stop at renaming it
Economist Trevor Tombe said the way Ottawa has characterized its action is a miscasting of what has happened, because it did not levy 50 per cent tariffs on the U.S. products it has targeted.
“They have called it ‘dollar-for-dollar’ retaliation, which is kind of stretching how we normally think about that,” Tombe told the Star.
“A good chunk of the trade that we’re retaliating on are using tariff rates of 15 and 25 per cent, whereas the U.S. rates are 50 (per cent),” he said. “The average tariff on the trade that we’re retaliating on is just over 30 per cent.”
Tombe estimates Canada’s counter-tariffs net out at about 60 cents to every dollar of American tariff.
“So when they say dollar-for-dollar retaliation, they don’t actually mean the total amount of tariffs. They mean the total amount of trade that is being affected by the tariffs.”
Tombe argued the goal should be to hit back while minimizing harm to Canadian companies and importers.
“It’s really hard for a small country to have meaningful retaliation in a well-targeted way without harming ourselves a great deal,” he said.

Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade negotiations fell apart on Friday. Both countries have accused each other of implementing eleventh-hour changes.

The lake's name "is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America," Carney added.
The relationship between Canada and the United States was already rocky before recent negotiations. Trump's tariffs and threats of annexation have angered and confused the historically close ally.
Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario Premier Doug Ford earlier this week.
The two exchanged insults, with Ford calling the president a bully, among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a "less charismatic, intelligent" version of his late brother, Rob.
Sitting near a map with the name "Lake America" over the body of water on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said Canada has been difficult to deal with and repeated claims the country was ripping off the United States.
"They want to be treated like a state but they are not a state," Trump said.
When asked why he was targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said "they haven't treated us well."
"The Canadian officials have treated us very badly," Trump said. "They are nasty people."
Ford said on social media Thursday that "it’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever."
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum — who previously was governor of border state North Dakota — posted on social media "the places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States." U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra shared Burgum's post.
But the renaming was quickly condemned as a distraction by others.
Republican Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont called the move disappointing. In a post on social media he said "we should be at the negotiating table, finding a path forward that strengthens both the U.S. and Canadian economies."
"Further escalating tensions does nothing to help American or Canadian families and businesses," Scott said.
Democrat Gov. Janet Mills of Maine posted a tip for the president on social media: "focus on lowering costs for your constituents instead of doodling on maps."
In Canada, the move prompted incredulity, with Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston posting on social media that "we're into some real foolishness now."
"It's Lake Ontario, buddy," Houston said.
At an unrelated news conference in Winnipeg, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew described the situation as an over-the-hill rock star playing old hits at a casino.
"I think that's the part of Donald Trump's presidency we're at now," Kinew said. "Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie with the Gulf of Mexico, and he's trying to bring back that, and he's trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it's a little sad and it's not his best work."
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said no executive order will change the lake's name and "it doesn't belong to President Donald Trump to rename on a whim." He said Canada should not respond to stunts and distractions and stay focused on what the country can control.
Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes — is located between Ontario and New York. The Canadian province is named after the lake.
The White House did not respond to questions about whether any Indigenous groups in the United States were consulted before the name change.
Trump pointed to his decision in 2025 to sign an executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, and mused that maybe next he'll change the name of the Atlantic or Pacific oceans.
The name change only applies to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services and American news agencies also made the change to the Gulf of Mexico.
The geographic controversy led to the White House removing The Associated Press from certain duties covering the president after the news service did not use "Gulf of America" in its reporting.

sources.text:

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed back against President Donald Trump’s order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” framing the response as part of Canada’s broader effort to withstand what he called unjustified American tariffs.
“In the face of unjustified American tariffs, Canadians have shown resolve, purpose, and strength,” Carney said in a post on X, adding that his government is “protecting Canadian workers, businesses, and families.”
Trump signed an executive order Thursday directing the U.S. government to use “Lake America” in its official geographic naming system, with the change taking effect immediately.
The president tied the renaming to his criticism of Canada’s trade policies, saying Canada had been “ripping us off for a long time on trade.”
The order adds a symbolic dispute over one of North America’s Great Lakes to a rapidly worsening trade relationship. The United States and Canada remain at odds after three days of negotiations ended without an agreement.
Following the collapse of the talks, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods. The duties apply to products including liquor, dairy, toys, clothing, electrical equipment and hockey gear.
Carney suspended the negotiations and said Canada would respond “dollar for dollar.”

The United States and Canada also maintain extensive trade in energy, agricultural products, metals and manufactured goods. Tariffs on Canadian materials and components could increase costs for American manufacturers, while duties on finished products could eventually be reflected in consumer prices.
The potential effect on affordability has become a political concern for Republicans as voters continue to focus on the cost of everyday goods.

Carney says it will always be Lake Ontario after Trump’s Lake America order
Written by The Canadian Press on August 27, 2026
WASHINGTON — Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canadians know Lake Ontario will always be known by its original name, after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change it to Lake America earlier today.
In a post on social media, Carney says the lake’s name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.
He says it’s a Wendat word which means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”
Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade negotiations fell apart on Friday.
Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario Premier Doug Ford earlier this week.
When asked by reporters in the Oval Office why he was targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said Canadians haven’t treated the U.S. well.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 27, 2026.
Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

Carney rejects Trump 'Lake America' order, vows to keep Lake Ontario
23:33, 27/08/2026, ThursdayU: Update: 23:48, 27/08/2026, Thursday

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney 
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday rejected US President Donald Trump's executive order renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America," insisting that Canadians will maintain the lake's historic Wendat-derived name amid escalating bilateral trade tensions.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday dismissed US President Donald Trump's executive order rebranding Lake Ontario as "Lake America," declaring that Canadians will continue to use the centuries-old name that predates both nations' founding documents.
Historical name predates both nations
Carney laid out the historical significance of the name in a post on X, noting that the designation carries more than 400 years of history. "The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big'," he said, explaining that the term predates both the Confederation of Canada and the American Declaration of Independence. Carney added that while Washington is changing its trading relationships, foreign policies and even hydronyms, Canadians remain committed to the lake's traditional designation — then, now and always.
Trump signs executive order
Trump formalized the renaming during a ceremony in the Oval Office, declaring that the change would take effect without delay. "We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately to 'Lake America'," he said before signing the executive order. The move comes as bilateral relations have deteriorated sharply over trade disputes.
Trade tensions escalate
Washington and Ottawa have exchanged punitive measures since the collapse of trade negotiations earlier this year, with the US imposing new tariffs on Canadian goods and Ottawa responding with retaliatory levies. The latest executive order on the lake's designation appears to mark another flashpoint in the deepening economic rift between the neighboring countries. Bilateral talks remain stalled as both sides maintain their respective tariff regimes.

sources.news_title: Lake America: Trump Renames Lake Ontario
sources.text:
Donald Trump turned his escalating dispute with Canada into a fight over the map Thursday, signing an executive order directing the federal government to call Lake Ontario “Lake America.” According to the White House executive order, the move applies to the body of water bordered by New York and the Canadian province of Ontario and makes the new designation the official name for U.S. federal use.
Video
Trump said the change was effective immediately, but the written order gives the Interior Department 30 days to carry out the administrative work. The White House order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to coordinate with the U.S. Board on Geographic Names, update the Geographic Names Information System, and remove references to Lake Ontario from that federal database. It also calls for federal maps, contracts, documents and communications to use Lake America.
That distinction matters because the order does not give Washington control over what Canada calls the shared lake. The U.S. Geological Survey says the Board on Geographic Names exists to standardize geographic names throughout the federal government. On the Canadian side, Ontario government naming policy identifies the Ontario Geographic Names Board as the province’s statutory authority for recommending names used on Ontario government documents, publications and maps. In other words, the U.S. can establish Lake America for federal use without changing Canada’s official terminology.
Private companies also are not automatically bound by the order. The U.S. Geological Survey’s guidance on nonfederal maps states that the federal government does not control how outside companies or organizations update their mapping products. There is still precedent for commercial adoption. After Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the “Gulf of America” in 2025, USGS later reported that the federal change had also appeared in commercial applications, including Google Maps and Apple Maps.
The Lake America announcement comes during a much broader economic confrontation. According to the Associated Press, Trump told reporters that Canada is “the worst” to deal with on trade. “They feel entitled, and we can’t have that,” he said. AP also reported that Trump had been discussing the lake name change in the days after negotiations between the two countries broke down.
The tariff fight carries much larger financial stakes than the naming dispute. According to Canada’s Department of Finance, new U.S. tariffs of 50 percent took effect August 22 on Canadian goods valued by Canada at $27.6 billion in Canadian dollars. Ottawa responded by announcing countermeasures covering the same value of U.S. imports. A separate Canadian government tariff schedule says those measures will take effect September 8 at rates of 15, 25 and 50 percent depending on the product.
The two economies remain deeply connected despite the political fight. The Office of the United States Trade Representative estimates total trade in goods and services between the U.S. and Canada reached $872.3 billion in 2025. That level of commerce makes the Lake America fight more than a random naming controversy because it is unfolding alongside a dispute involving one of America’s biggest trading relationships.
Ontario itself is especially important to American exporters. In a 2024 fiscal statement using 2023 trade data, the Ontario government said the province was the top export destination for 17 U.S. states and ranked second for another 11. Ontario also reported roughly $500 billion in total trade with the United States that year, illustrating how closely factories, suppliers and consumers on both sides of the border remain connected.
Geographically, the new U.S. label applies to a lake that neither country controls alone. According to the Canada Water Agency, Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area at 18,960 square kilometers, and the international border runs through the lake between Ontario and New York. Reuters reported that roughly 52 percent of the lake’s surface area lies on the Canadian side.
The name change also does not alter the international boundary or the longstanding framework for managing the shared water system. The International Joint Commission says the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909 was created to help Canada and the United States prevent and resolve disputes involving waters they share. The Lake America executive order addresses federal naming practices and contains no provision changing the border, treaty obligations, or the two countries’ jurisdiction over the water.
The history behind the word Ontario adds another layer to the controversy. The Associated Press traces the lake’s name to the Huron Indigenous word “oniatarí:io,” meaning “lake of shining waters,” and notes that the name predates European settlement. Ontario government sources describe the linguistic origin somewhat differently. The province’s current official history page says Ontario comes from the Iroquois word “kanadario,” meaning “sparkling” water, while an earlier Ontario government language resource connects the name to a Mohawk form, “Oniatari’:io,” meaning beautiful lake. The sources differ on the precise language and translation, but they consistently identify Ontario as a name with Indigenous roots that existed long before the modern U.S. and Canada.
The clash is also part of a longer deterioration in political relations between the neighboring countries. The Associated Press reported that Trump has repeatedly suggested Canada could become the 51st state, an idea Canadian leaders have rejected, while his administration has used tariffs and other trade threats during the dispute. The Lake Ontario proposal initially surfaced publicly on Tuesday before becoming an executive order two days later.
Canadian officials had already indicated they would not adopt the Lake America name. Before Thursday’s signing, Canadian Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said, “We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period.” according to Reuters. As of Thursday afternoon, Reuters reported that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office had not immediately responded to the signed order, leaving the United States with a new federal name for a shared lake that Canada still officially recognizes as Lake Ontario.
